title: Comparatives: -er vs more
question: My house is ___ than yours.
explanation: Short adjectives (one syllable) add -er. Big becomes bigger (double the final consonant). 'More big' and 'more bigger' are wrong, and 'biger' is a spelling error.

title: Comparatives: -er vs more
question: This book is ___ than that one.
explanation: Long adjectives use 'more' before the adjective for comparisons: more interesting than. 'Most' is for superlatives, 'interested' describes a person, and 'as interesting' needs 'as' after it.

title: Comparatives: irregular
question: She is ___ at tennis than me.
explanation: 'Good' has an irregular comparative: good, better. 'Good' is the base form, 'best' is the superlative, and 'more good' is not used.

title: Comparatives: -er vs more
question: This street is ___ than the one near the park.
explanation: Short adjectives add -er: narrow becomes narrower. We cannot add 'more' as well, and 'narrowest' and 'most narrow' are superlatives.

title: Comparatives: sentence structure
question: The weather today is much ___ than yesterday.
explanation: One-syllable adjectives use -er for comparatives. 'Much' adds emphasis: much colder. 'More colder' doubles the comparative, 'coldest' is a superlative, and 'as cold' needs 'as' after it.

title: Superlatives: -est vs most
question: She is the ___ student in the class.
explanation: One-syllable adjectives use -est for superlatives: smart becomes smartest. 'Most smartest' and 'more smartest' double the superlative, and 'smarter' compares only two.

title: Superlatives: -est vs most
question: That was the ___ film I have ever seen.
explanation: Long adjectives use 'most' for superlatives: boring becomes most boring. 'More boring' is a comparative, 'bored' describes a feeling and 'boringest' is not used.

title: Superlatives: irregular
question: This is the ___ pizza in town.
explanation: 'Good' has an irregular superlative: good, better, best. 'Better' is the comparative, and 'most good' and 'goodest' are not used.

title: Superlatives: irregular
question: That was the ___ day of my life.
explanation: 'Bad' has an irregular superlative: bad, worse, worst. 'Worse' is the comparative, and 'most bad' and 'most worst' are not used.

title: Superlatives: sentence structure
question: Mount Everest is the ___ mountain in the world.
explanation: One-syllable adjectives use -est for superlatives: high becomes highest. 'Higher' is the comparative, and 'most high' and 'most highest' are not used.

title: First conditional: if clause
question: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay home.
explanation: In the first conditional, the 'if' clause uses the present simple, not 'will' or 'would'. If + present simple, will + base verb.

title: First conditional: result clause
question: If you study hard, you ___ the exam.
explanation: In the first conditional, the result clause uses 'will' + base verb: will pass. 'Would pass' belongs to the second conditional, and 'passes' does not agree with 'you'.

title: First conditional: if clause
question: If she ___ early, she will catch the bus.
explanation: The 'if' clause in a first conditional uses present simple: If she leaves... 'Will leave' and 'left' are the wrong tenses, and 'leave' does not agree with 'she'.

title: First conditional: negative
question: If you ___ eat breakfast, you will be hungry later.
explanation: In the first conditional, the 'if' clause uses present simple. With 'you', the negative is 'don't' + base verb.

title: First conditional: result clause
question: If we miss the train, we ___ late for the meeting.
explanation: The result clause of a first conditional uses 'will' + base verb: we will be late. 'Would be' belongs to the second conditional, and 'were' and 'been' are not used here.

title: First conditional: unless
question: '___ you hurry, you will miss the flight.' Which word completes it?
explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': Unless you hurry = If you don't hurry. 'If you hurry, you will miss the flight' would mean the opposite.

title: First conditional: complete
question: If I ___ enough money, I will buy a new phone.
explanation: The 'if' clause uses present simple: If I have enough money. 'Will have' is not used in the 'if' clause, and 'had' and 'would have' belong to other conditionals.

title: First conditional: result clause
question: If the weather is nice, we ___ to the beach.
explanation: The result clause in a first conditional uses 'will' + base verb: we will go. 'Would go' belongs to the second conditional, and 'went' and 'gone' are not used here.

title: Adverbs of frequency: position
question: My brother ___ at home on Saturdays. He is always out.
explanation: Adverbs of frequency go after the verb 'be': He is never at home. 'Never is' puts the adverb before 'be', and 'isn't never' is a double negative.

title: Adverbs of frequency: position
question: I ___ go to the gym on Mondays.
explanation: 'Usually' is an adverb of frequency. It goes before the main verb: I usually go.

title: Adverbs of frequency: position
question: He ___ drinks coffee in the morning.
explanation: 'Always' goes before the main verb: He always drinks. ('Is always' is used with 'be', not with other verbs.)

title: Adverbs of frequency: meaning
question: We ___ eat out. Maybe once or twice a year.
explanation: 'Hardly ever' means almost never. Once or twice a year = very rare.

title: Adverbs of frequency: position
question: They are ___ happy to help.
explanation: With the verb 'be', adverbs of frequency go after it: They are always happy. 'Every time', 'all the time' and 'whenever' cannot stand before an adjective like this.

title: Adverbs of degree: too
question: This coffee is ___ hot to drink.
explanation: 'Too' + adjective + 'to' means 'more than is good or possible'. Too hot to drink = you cannot drink it. 'Enough' follows an adjective, and 'so' and 'such' do not fit before 'to drink' here.

title: Adverbs of degree: very vs too
question: The film was ___ long, but I still enjoyed it.
explanation: 'Very' is neutral emphasis. Use 'very' before an adjective to intensify it. 'Enough' follows an adjective, and 'much' and 'more' cannot go before 'long' here.

title: Adverbs of degree: quite
question: The test was ___ difficult, but most students passed.
explanation: 'Quite' means 'fairly' or 'somewhat'. It goes before the adjective: quite difficult. 'Too' would suggest the test was impossible, and 'enough' and 'much' do not fit before 'difficult'.

title: Adverbs of degree: really
question: I am ___ tired today. I need to sleep more.
explanation: 'Really' is an adverb that means 'very'. 'Too much' and 'so many' are used with nouns or verbs, not with adjectives like 'tired', and 'enough' follows an adjective.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: enjoy
question: I enjoy ___ in the park.
explanation: After 'enjoy', we always use the gerund (-ing form): enjoy walking, enjoy reading.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: want
question: She wants ___ a doctor.
explanation: After 'want', we always use the infinitive (to + verb): want to become.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: avoid
question: You should avoid ___ too much sugar.
explanation: After 'avoid', we always use the gerund (-ing form): avoid eating.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: decide
question: They decided ___ to Paris for the holiday.
explanation: After 'decide', we use the infinitive (to + verb): decided to go.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: finish
question: Have you finished ___ your homework?
explanation: After 'finish', we use the gerund (-ing form): finish doing.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: hope
question: I hope ___ you again soon.
explanation: After 'hope', we use the infinitive (to + verb): hope to see.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: mind
question: Do you mind ___ the window?
explanation: After 'mind', we use the gerund (-ing form): Do you mind opening...?

title: Gerund vs infinitive: learn
question: He is learning ___ the guitar.
explanation: After 'learn', we use the infinitive (to + verb): learning to play.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: suggest
question: She suggested ___ a movie tonight.
explanation: After 'suggest', we use the gerund (-ing form): suggested watching.

title: Gerund vs infinitive: promise
question: He promised ___ me with my project.
explanation: After 'promise', we use the infinitive (to + verb): promised to help.

title: Too and enough: too + adjective
question: He is ___ young to drive a car.
explanation: 'Too' + adjective + 'to' means something is more than the acceptable level. Too young to drive = he cannot drive. 'Enough' follows an adjective, and 'such' and 'much' do not fit here.

title: Too and enough: adjective + enough
question: She is ___ to ride the roller coaster.
explanation: 'Enough' comes after the adjective: tall enough (not 'enough tall'). 'Taller enough' and 'tall too' are not used.

title: Too and enough: enough + noun
question: We don't have ___ to finish the project.
explanation: 'Enough' comes before an uncountable noun: enough time. 'Time' here is uncountable, so 'times' is wrong, and 'enough of' and 'too' do not fit.

title: Too and enough: too much
question: There is ___ noise in here. I can't concentrate.
explanation: 'Too much' is used with uncountable nouns. Noise is uncountable, so we say 'too much noise'. 'Too many' and 'too few' are for countable nouns, and 'too little' would mean not enough noise.

title: Too and enough: too many
question: There are ___ people on the bus. Let's wait for the next one.
explanation: 'Too many' is used with countable plural nouns. People is countable, so we say 'too many people'. 'Too much' and 'too little' are for uncountable nouns, and 'too few' would mean not enough people.

title: Too and enough: not + adjective + enough
question: This bag is ___ for all my books.
explanation: 'Not' + adjective + 'enough': not big enough. 'Enough' always comes after the adjective.

title: Comparatives: as...as
question: Tom is ___ his brother.
explanation: We use 'as + adjective + as' to say two things are equal: as tall as. 'Than' is used with comparatives, not with 'as'.

title: Comparatives: less
question: This exercise is ___ than the last one.
explanation: 'Less' is the opposite of 'more'. Less difficult = not as difficult. 'Least' is a superlative, 'fewer' is for countable nouns and 'lesser' is not used before an adjective.

title: First conditional: question
question: What will you do if you ___ the job?
explanation: In first conditional questions, the 'if' clause uses present simple: if you don't get.

title: Adverbs of degree: enough as adverb
question: He didn't run fast ___ to win the race.
explanation: 'Enough' as an adverb goes after the adjective or adverb: fast enough. 'Too', 'very' and 'so' cannot follow 'fast' here.

title: Gerund: after preposition
question: She is good ___ languages.
explanation: After an adjective + preposition, we use the gerund: good at learning. 'At' is the preposition used with 'good', and the verb after it must be -ing.

title: Superlatives: one of the
question: Paris is one of ___ cities in Europe.
explanation: 'One of the + superlative + plural noun' is the correct pattern. Long adjectives use 'most', and 'the' is needed. 'More' is a comparative.

title: Too and enough: enough with verb
question: I didn't sleep ___. I'm exhausted.
explanation: 'Enough' can follow a verb to mean 'a sufficient amount': didn't sleep enough. 'Too', 'very' and 'such' cannot end this sentence.
